walkthroughs.body_html:
The four classic aims are retribution, deterrence, reformation and protection.

Retribution: 'an eye for an eye' (Exodus 21:24) — proportional payback.

Deterrence: discourage the offender and others.

Reformation: rehabilitate so they don't reoffend. Protection: keep the public safe.

Key causes studied at GCSE include: poverty, upbringing, mental illness, addiction, greed, peer pressure, and opposition to unjust law (e.g. civil rights activists).

Christianity teaches we have free will but live in a fallen world. Islam teaches Allah will judge intentions on the Last Day.

A crime breaks the law of the land; a sin breaks God's law. They often overlap (e.g. murder) but not always — lying is usually a sin but not always a crime.

Some acts (e.g. apartheid laws) were legal but sinful; some acts (e.g. helping refugees illegally) may be legal crimes but moral duties.

mcqs.q: When was UK capital punishment abolished?
How many aims of punishment are commonly listed?
What do orthodox Christians believe about the nature of Jesus?
options: Karma is a god who decides what happens to you.
Jesus was half God and half human.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.
He is fully God and fully human at the same time (the incarnation) — both natures united in one person, as defined at the Council of Chalcedon.

mcqs.q: What does karma mean in Hindu and Buddhist thought?
options: The Buddha created the universe.
The principle that actions have moral consequences shaping future experience or rebirth — not fate, but ethical cause and effect built into reality.
Karma is when bad things happen to bad people as punishment.
Karma is a god who decides what happens to you.

mcqs.q: Is the Buddha a god in Buddhism?
options: The Buddha created the universe.
Buddhists worship the Buddha as their god.
Jesus was a human who became God after his resurrection.

No — the Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama) is regarded as an enlightened human teacher who discovered the path to liberation. Theravada Buddhism is generally non-theistic; some Mahayana traditions develop more elaborate cosmologies.
